newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya frustrates UNEP's efforts to cut costs.
newsitem.headline: Kenya frustrates UNEP's efforts to cut costs.

text.p: Kenya is frustrating efforts by the Nairobi-based U.N. environment agency to cut costs and improve its information system, agency officials said on Monday.

The officials, speaking on the sidelines of the Governing Council of the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP), told Reuters the Kenyan government's failure to authorise advanced, cost-saving satellite system was playing into the hands of mainly Western donors who want UNEP headquarters moved from Nairobi.
UNEP is the only U.N. agency based in the developing world.

"The Governing Council expresses its grave concern that the government of Kenya has not yet authorised the submission of the necessary documentation to enable UNEP to initiate operation of this advanced system," a UNEP statement said.
No Kenyan officials were available to comment. The council approved the satellite telecommunications network in 1995.

The UNEP officials said Kenya's reluctance was based on fears the new system would hit the state-owned Kenya Posts and Telecommunications Corporation (KPTC), which receives $5 million annually from UNEP for phone bills.
Experts at the Nairobi meeting -- attended by ministers and representatives from 100 countries -- said the satellite system would cut UNEP's communications bill by half.
"This is a huge cost-saving measure, more so because key donors are no longer willing or are reluctant to give out more money to agencies like UNEP," an Asian diplomat said.
UNEP is reeling from financial woes caused by unpaid dues from Western donors demanding reform and cost-saving measures.
Key Western donors such as Japan, United States of America, Britain, France and Italy are reluctant to pay, arguing UNEP has become less effective since the 1992 Earth Summit.
As a result UNEP has seen its budget drop sharply over the last few years as donors link funding to reforms in the agency.
Other delegates at the meeting described the failure to approve the system as a political blunder because Kenya makes large amounts of money from UNEP's presence in Nairobi.
"By refusing to allow UNEP to modernise its telecommunications system, thereby cutting costs, Kenya is playing into the hands of reform-minded donors," an African delegate said.
"Donors have always wanted UNEP to move away from Kenya and in essence from the developing world and poor communications offers a perfect excuse," he added.
Donors complain Kenya's telecommunications network is poor, expensive and hinders UNEP's ability to function efficiently.
The issue is particularly sensitive this year because of the United States' determination to cut funding to U.N. agencies it considers wasteful, inefficient and outdated.
